A1.justification: Despite the changed title and expanded scope, both PDFs describe the same underlying probing study. The complete main texts and appendices support matching the retained methods, datasets, results, equations, and figures.

before.justification: v3 reports original multilingual lemma and inflection probing results, together with attention, steering, tokenization, dimensionality, and pretraining-checkpoint analyses.

after.justification: v4 retains those empirical results and adds original probing results for eight English linguistic tasks, including accuracy, selectivity, layer-depth summaries, and model correlations.

M1.justification: v4 Section 2.1 extends the word-level probing procedure with mean-pooled span representations and pair features combining two representations, their product, and their absolute difference. This is a limited procedural adaptation; the existing ridge, MLP, random-forest, and steering methods remain.

E1.justification: v4 adds POS, dependencies, constituents, named entities, semantic roles, semantic proto-roles, coreference, and relation classification. Section 3.1 introduces corresponding English coverage through GUM annotations, Universal Propositions English-EWT, SPR1, and SemEval-2010 Task 8, while retaining the six-language lemma and inflection study.

E2.justification: The model roster in Table 1 and comparator membership in the retained experiments are unchanged. Linear regression, MLPs, and inflection-only random forests remain the comparison methods. The added pipeline tasks use existing linear and MLP probes; cited edge-probing and scalar-mixing approaches are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The added task suite introduces token/span/edge evaluation and new depth-localization metrics: Expected Layer and Center of Gravity. v4 also compares vectorized task-by-layer accuracy profiles using Pearson correlations. Existing classifier hyperparameters and training budgets are retained in Appendix C; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 Figure 2 adds a cross-model correlation analysis testing whether accuracy profiles group by architecture and model size. The existing tokenization comparison, attention-versus-residual analysis, steering-strength tests, dimensionality analysis, checkpoint comparisons, and error breakdowns remain; their relocation does not constitute new analyses.

E5.justification: v4 adds statistical association estimates through Pearson correlations between model accuracy profiles in Figure 2. This is a limited statistics addition: neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and no new run-to-run uncertainty estimation is documented.

E6.justification: v4 adds extensive pipeline-task accuracy, selectivity, depth-summary, and correlation results. For example, Figure 3 reports BERT-Base relation accuracy of 38.8% for linear probes and 19.5% for MLPs, with negative selectivity. These are newly reported tasks, not same-setting improvements. All 19 detailed result tables in v3 Tables 7–25 match v4 Tables 8–26 numerically.

T1.justification: v4 Equations 6–7 introduce formal definitions of Center of Gravity and Expected Layer using cumulative best accuracy and normalized layer weights or increments. These add mathematical definitions beyond v3; the classifier and steering equations are retained, and no substantial theorem or proof development is added.

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from lexical identity and inflectional morphology to the claim that modern models rediscover a syntax-to-semantics-to-discourse pipeline. v4 also claims that larger contemporary models develop useful linguistic representations earlier. The original multilingual findings remain, but become a focused study within this broader argument.

C2.justification: v4 Sections 4.2–4.3 add the interpretation that greater capacity and stronger pretraining compress linguistic stages toward earlier layers. They also interpret selectivity as validating the pipeline findings, despite negative discourse-task selectivity in Figures 3 and 10. The four existing limitations are retained in Appendix A rather than substantively revised.

D1.justification: v4 adds a reproducibility statement describing the existing repository's dataset-construction, probing, and plotting code, and explicitly states that activations are frozen. However, v3's specified 70/10/20 split stratified by inflection labels disappears. The classifier hyperparameters are relocated unchanged to Appendix C, and the repository address is retained.

R1.justification: v4 substantially repositions the paper as a modern-model extension of the classical NLP pipeline literature. Section 2.1 explicitly adopts Tenney et al.'s edge-probing design while distinguishing independent-layer probes from scalar mixing. It adds Tenney et al. (2019b) and Jindal et al. (2022), while removing the Ansuini and Ismayilzada citations.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around the pipeline question. The previous Results and Analysis sections are condensed into Section 5, probe design and metrics are reorganized, and limitations, training details, and dimensionality material move into reorganized appendices.

P2.justification: v4 replaces the two-column layout with a single-column format, adds pipeline heatmaps, correlation displays, and depth-summary grids, and redraws many retained plots with changed typography, legends, and axes. For example, checkpoint accuracy plots now use full 0–1 axes. Existing dataset distributions are relabeled from a figure to a table.

improvement.justification: The added task-level evidence and explicit depth metrics make the broader pipeline hypothesis directly inspectable. However, Section 4.2 treats controls as supportive despite negative discourse selectivity, including BERT-Base relation MLP selectivity of -58.9 in Figure 3. The omission of the earlier split ratio also weakens reproducibility. These evidentiary gains and interpretation/reporting problems prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
